Thumb
thum
noun
From the Saxon thuma, the short thick finger set opposite the rest; rendering the Hebrew bohen yad, literally the thumb of the hand, the member without which the hand can grasp nothing.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The thumb is the member that makes a hand a hand: without it the fingers close on nothing. Scripture gives it a fixed and remarkable place in the ritual of consecration. At the ordaining of Aaron and his sons the blood of the ram was put “upon the tip of the right ear… and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot” (Exo 29:20), and Moses did precisely so at the altar (Lev 8:24). The identical rite is performed over the cleansed leper, blood and then oil upon ear, thumb, and toe (Lev 14:14), so that a man restored to the camp is consecrated by the same three touches that ordain a priest. The three members are not chosen at random. The ear is what he hears, the thumb is what he does, the great toe is where he walks; blood upon them claims hearing, working, and walking — the whole man, and the right side of him, his readiest strength. Nothing is left to the man’s own disposal. The dark inversion of the figure stands in Judges: the seventy kings whose thumbs and great toes Adoni-bezek had cut off, gathering meat under his table, until his own thumbs and toes were taken and he confessed, “as I have done, so God hath requited me” (Jdg 1:6–7). To take a man’s thumbs is to unmake his labour; to bloody a man’s thumb at the altar is to claim it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The short thick finger of the hand, set opposite the others; in the Levitical rites one of the three members — ear, thumb, and great toe — touched with blood in consecration and cleansing.

THUMB, n. The short thick finger of the human hand, or the corresponding member of an animal.

Saxon thuma; allied to the Latin pollex, the finger of strength.

It is set opposite the other fingers, and by it the hand grasps and holds; hence a figure for capacity to labour.

Hebrew bohen, used of both the thumb of the hand and the great toe of the foot.

Anointed with blood at the consecration of priests (Exo 29:20; Lev 8:24) and at the cleansing of the leper (Lev 14:14).

Key Scripture

Exo 29:20 — "Then shalt thou kill the ram, and take of his blood, and put it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot, and sprinkle the blood upon the altar round about."

Lev 8:24 — "And he brought Aaron's sons, and Moses put of the blood upon the tip of their right ear, and upon the thumbs of their right hands, and upon the great toes of their right feet: and Moses sprinkled the blood upon the altar round about."

Lev 14:14 — "And the priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and the priest shall put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot:"

Jdg 1:6 — "But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes."

Modern Corruption

The live misuse is partial consecration — a religion of the ear that never reaches the thumb, hearing much and doing little, as though God claimed a compartment of a man rather than the whole of him.

expand to see more

The abiding temptation the thumb exposes is a consecration that stops at the ear. Blood was put on three members, not one, and the order is instructive: hearing first, because faith comes by hearing, then the working hand and the walking foot, because a hearing that never reaches the hand is what James calls deceiving one’s own self. Modern religious life has a settled habit of dividing a man into a sacred compartment and a secular one — sermons, songs, and devotions on the one side; trade, labour, money, and the ordinary week on the other — and of supposing God has claimed the first and left the second to the man’s own discretion. The Levitical rite forbids that division at the outset. It is the right thumb, the strong working member of the strong hand, that is bloodied at the altar; a man’s craft, his contract, his tools, and his wages are consecrated ground. The same three touches are laid on the cleansed leper, which is to say that the man brought back from exclusion is not merely permitted to rejoin the camp but claimed for service in it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that redemption claims the entire man, body and soul, and claims him by blood. “Ye are not your own… for ye are bought with a price” (1Co 6:19–20) is the New Testament of the ear, thumb, and toe. Christ our great High Priest was consecrated to a work that used every member — ears open to the Father’s will, hands that healed and were pierced, feet that went about doing good and were nailed — and He gives His people the same undivided consecration. So the believer yields his members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), which is a whole-body doctrine, not a sentiment. Adoni-bezek stands at the other pole as a warning of exact retribution: he unmade seventy men’s hands and lost his own, and he knew the ledger was God’s. The thumb that God claims at the altar, God may also require at the judgment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The grasping member of the hand; with ear and great toe, one of the three parts touched with blood to consecrate the whole man.

expand to see more

Thumb — Saxon thuma, the thick finger by which the hand grasps.

Hebrew bohen, used alike of the thumb and the great toe.

Ear, thumb, toe: what a man hears, what he does, where he walks.

The right side is specified — the readiest strength is claimed first.

The same rite ordains a priest (Exo 29:20) and restores a leper (Lev 14:14).

Usage

"Blood on the thumb consecrates a man’s labour, not merely his devotions."

"The leper is cleansed by the priest’s own ordination rite — restored and claimed in one act."

"Adoni-bezek’s severed thumbs are exact requital; he confessed the justice himself."
